planting.note: Direct sow 1-2 inches deep after last frost in well-drained soil; Greasy Grits is a pole-type Appalachian heirloom needing a trellis, teepee, or corn stalks to climb.

directions: Sow seeds 1-2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a sturdy trellis, pole, or teepee for the vigorous climbing vines; Greasy Grits is one of the many named strains of Appalachian greasy bean, so called for the smooth, shiny, almost oil-slick sheen on the pod surface caused by a lack of the fine fuzz found on most snap beans. Pods are stringless and tender when picked young for snapping, with a rich, savory flavor prized in traditional mountain cooking, and the plant can also be left to mature for shelling as a dry bean. Like other greasy beans it is a genuine landrace maintained by generations of Appalachian seed savers rather than a modern breeding-program release, so some variation between seed lots is normal and part of its heirloom character. Provide consistent moisture through pod set and pick regularly to keep the vigorous vine productive over a long summer harvest window.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12-14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August-September for fall and winter production. Green Glaze's waxy, glossy leaf coating gives it unusually strong resistance to cabbage worms and other leaf-feeding pests.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Green Glaze is a Southern heirloom collard distinguished by unusually smooth, thick, glossy, jade-green leaves with a waxy cuticle that makes it noticeably more resistant to cabbage worms, cabbage loopers, and other leaf-chewing pests than standard fuzzy-leaved collard varieties, an especially useful trait for organic growers. The flavor is mild and sweet for a collard, and the smooth leaf texture that deters pests also makes the leaves pleasant for fresh use in wraps as well as traditional slow-cooked greens. Like other collards it tolerates both summer heat and considerable cold, with flavor sweetening noticeably after the first light frosts of fall. Harvest outer leaves as needed and the plant continues producing new growth from the top through a long cool-season harvest window.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Collard Production in the Southeast

common_name: Alabama Blue Collards (Southern Heirloom Blue-Green Collard)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12-14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August-September for fall and winter production. Alabama Blue is a traditional open-pollinated Deep South collard passed down through generations of home gardeners.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Alabama Blue is a traditional open-pollinated Deep South collard with broad, slightly savoyed, distinctly blue-green leaves, maintained and passed down through generations of Southern home gardeners rather than developed by a commercial breeding program. The flavor is rich and full-bodied even before frost, and like other collards sweetens further after the first light freezes of fall. Plants are tall and vigorous, tolerating both Gulf South summer heat and winter cold well, and the open-pollinated nature means seed can be saved from the best plants each year to maintain the strain in a home garden. Harvest the lower and outer leaves as needed, leaving the growing tip intact so the plant keeps producing fresh leaves from the top over a long cool-season harvest window.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Collard Production in the Southeast

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12-14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August-September for fall and winter production. Yellow Cabbage Collards form an unusually loose, pale yellow-green head rather than the open rosette typical of most collards.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Yellow Cabbage Collards are a distinctive Southern heirloom type that blurs the line between collards and cabbage, forming a loose, blanched, pale yellow-green head at the center of the plant rather than the fully open rosette of leaves typical of most collard varieties. The blanched inner leaves are notably tender and mild, sweeter and less assertively cabbage-flavored than standard collards, making this variety popular for gardeners who find ordinary collards too strong. Like other collards it tolerates considerable cold and its flavor improves after light fall frosts. Because the plant's value lies partly in the self-blanched head, avoid stripping too many outer leaves early in the season and let the center fill in before beginning regular harvest, then continue picking outer leaves as the plant keeps producing from the growing point.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Collard Production in the Southeast

common_name: Ole Timey Blue Collards (Traditional Southern Heirloom Collard)
scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. acephala 'Ole Timey Blue'

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12-14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August-September for fall and winter production. Ole Timey Blue is a tall, vigorous, open-pollinated Southern heirloom maintained by generations of home seed savers.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Ole Timey Blue is a tall, vigorous, open-pollinated Southern heirloom collard with broad, blue-green leaves, representing the traditional dooryard collard type grown throughout the Deep South long before modern compact hybrids became widely available. Plants grow quite tall over a long season, and the leaves carry the classic robust, full-bodied collard flavor that sweetens further after the first light fall frosts. Because it is a genuine open-pollinated landrace rather than a stabilized commercial variety, some plant-to-plant variation in leaf shape and color is normal and part of its heirloom character, and seed can be saved from the best plants to maintain the strain. Harvest outer and lower leaves as needed, leaving the central growing point intact so the plant continues producing fresh leaves from the top through a long cool-season harvest.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Collard Production in the Southeast
